questions.prompt: What does the identity matrix do to a vector \(\mathbf v\)?
questions.answer:
The identity matrix leaves every vector unchanged:
\[
I\mathbf v=\mathbf v.
\]
It represents the linear map that makes no geometric change.

questions.prompt: State the defining condition for a symmetric matrix.
questions.answer:
A square matrix is symmetric when it equals its transpose:
\[
A^T=A.
\]
This means entries mirror across the main diagonal.

questions.prompt: Compute \(D(3,-2)\) for \(D=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer:
A diagonal matrix scales coordinates separately:
\[
D(3,-2)=(4\cdot3,(-1)(-2))=(12,2).
\]

questions.prompt: Is \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&5\\5&2\end{pmatrix}\) symmetric?
questions.answer: Yes. The off-diagonal entries match: the \((1,2)\) entry is \(5\) and the \((2,1)\) entry is also \(5\). Therefore \(A^T=A\).

questions.prompt: Show that \(P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) is a projection matrix.
questions.answer:
Compute its square:
\[
P^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=P.
\]
Since \(P^2=P\), applying it twice has the same effect as applying it once, so it is a projection.

questions.prompt: Find the transpose of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer:
Rows become columns:
\[
A^T=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\2&5\\3&6\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The original was \(2\times3\), so the transpose is \(3\times2\).

questions.prompt: What geometric action does \(R=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) perform on \((x,y)\)?
questions.answer:
Multiply:
\[
R(x,y)=(-y,x).
\]
This sends \((1,0)\) to \((0,1)\) and \((0,1)\) to \((-1,0)\), so it is a rotation by \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise.

questions.prompt: Check whether \(Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) is orthogonal.
questions.answer:
Since \(Q^T=Q\), compute
\[
Q^TQ=Q^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=I.
\]
Therefore \(Q\) is orthogonal.

questions.prompt: For \(D=\operatorname{diag}(2,-3,5)\), compute \(D(x,y,z)\) and describe the action.
questions.answer:
The diagonal entries scale the matching coordinates:
\[
D(x,y,z)=(2x,-3y,5z).
\]
So the \(x\)-direction is stretched by \(2\), the \(y\)-direction is reversed and stretched by \(3\), and the \(z\)-direction is stretched by \(5\).

questions.prompt: Show that the zero matrix sends every vector to zero.
questions.answer:
Let \(0_{m\times n}\) be the zero matrix. Multiplying by \(\mathbf v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) gives each output component as a sum of zeros:
\[
0v_1+0v_2+\cdots+0v_n=0.
\]
Thus \(0_{m\times n}\mathbf v=\mathbf0\) for every input vector.

questions.prompt: Verify that an orthogonal matrix preserves lengths, using \(Q^TQ=I\).
questions.answer:
The squared length of \(Q\mathbf v\) is
\[
(Q\mathbf v)\cdot(Q\mathbf v)=(Q\mathbf v)^T(Q\mathbf v)=\mathbf v^TQ^TQ\mathbf v.
\]
Since \(Q^TQ=I\), this becomes
\[
\mathbf v^TI\mathbf v=\mathbf v^T\mathbf v=\lVert\mathbf v\rVert^2.
\]
So lengths are preserved.

questions.prompt: Explain why \(P^2=P\) means a projection does not change after being applied once.
questions.answer:
If \(P\) is applied to \(\mathbf v\), the result is \(P\mathbf v\). Applying \(P\) again gives
\[
P(P\mathbf v)=P^2\mathbf v.
\]
If \(P^2=P\), then this equals \(P\mathbf v\). Thus the second application makes no further change.

questions.prompt: For which \(a\) is \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&a\\3&2\end{pmatrix}\) symmetric?
questions.answer:
For symmetry, the off-diagonal entries must match. Thus the \((1,2)\) entry \(a\) must equal the \((2,1)\) entry \(3\). Therefore
\[
a=3.
\]

questions.prompt: Find all \(k\) such that \(P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&k\end{pmatrix}\) is a projection.
questions.answer:
A projection satisfies \(P^2=P\). Compute
\[
P^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&k^2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Equating with \(P\) gives \(k^2=k\). Hence
\[
k(k-1)=0,
\]
so \(k=0\) or \(k=1\).

questions.prompt: For which \(c\) is \(Q=\begin{pmatrix}c&0\\0&c\end{pmatrix}\) orthogonal?
questions.answer:
Orthogonality requires \(Q^TQ=I\). Since \(Q=cI\),
\[
Q^TQ=(cI)^T(cI)=c^2I.
\]
Set \(c^2I=I\), so \(c^2=1\). Therefore
\[
c=1\quad\text{or}\quad c=-1.
\]

questions.prompt: Classify \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\) as symmetric, diagonal, orthogonal, or projection where applicable.
questions.answer:
It is not diagonal because it has non-zero off-diagonal entries. It is not symmetric because \(A^T=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\ne A\). Check orthogonal:
\[
A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}=I.
\]
So it is orthogonal. Also \(A^2=-I\), so it is not a projection.

questions.prompt: A diagonal matrix \(D\) satisfies \(D(1,0)=(3,0)\) and \(D(0,1)=(0,-2)\). Find \(D\) and \(D(4,5)\).
questions.answer:
The basis outputs give the diagonal entries, so
\[
D=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then
\[
D(4,5)=(12,-10).
\]

questions.prompt: A student says every matrix with many zeros is diagonal. Give a counterexample and explain.
questions.answer:
A diagonal matrix can have non-zero entries only on the main diagonal. The matrix
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&5\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
\]
has three zeros, but the non-zero entry \(5\) is off the main diagonal. Therefore \(A\) is sparse but not diagonal.

questions.prompt: Prove that the product of two diagonal \(2\times2\) matrices is diagonal.
questions.answer:
Let
\[
D_1=\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_2=\begin{pmatrix}c&0\\0&d\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then
\[
D_1D_2=\begin{pmatrix}ac&0\\0&bd\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The off-diagonal entries are still zero, so the product is diagonal.

questions.prompt: Explain why the determinant test for invertibility cannot be applied to a \(2\times3\) zero matrix.
questions.answer: The determinant is defined only for square matrices. A \(2\times3\) matrix maps \(\mathbb R^3\) to \(\mathbb R^2\), so input and output dimensions differ. Since it is not square, \(\det A\) is not defined, and determinant-based invertibility tests do not apply.
